text.content:
Making a character takes about ten minutes. You choose (or roll for) your animal, decide what you’re good at as a person, and pick one small thing that shows in both your shapes. If you’d rather start straight away, take one of the six ready-made Bonded in Chapter 18.

Making a Character, Step by Step

  1. Frame and animal. Choose them, or roll a d6 for your frame (the table below) and a d6 for your animal: 1–2 is the first animal listed, 3–4 the second, 5–6 the third. No two characters in a group have the same animal. If two players want the same one, they each roll a die and the higher roll gets it (roll again on a tie); the other picks again (they can keep the same frame). Copy your frame’s animal ratings (Wits 0), its Strengths and Weaknesses, and your animal’s perk onto your sheet.
  2. Human ratings. Put 3, 2, 2, 1 and 1 into Sneak, Force, Move, Sense and Wits.
  3. Human perk. Choose one, or roll two d6.
  4. Your Mark. One feature that shows in both forms.
  5. The rest. A name, an age (11 to 15), and something you love about your town. Start every mission with 4 Wild and 0 Hurt.

The Five Approaches

Everything you try is done with one of five approaches. Each has a rating from 0 to 4: the number of dice you roll.

ApproachWhat it covers
SneakHiding, stalking, slipping past, staying unseen.
ForceFighting, breaking, shoving, scaring.
MoveRunning, climbing, jumping, flying, swimming.
SenseNoticing, tracking, searching, scouting.
WitsTalking, planning out loud, using tools and machines, reading. Human form only.

You have two sets of ratings. As a human, you use the five you chose in step 2. As an animal, you use your frame’s ratings instead, and your Wits is 0: animals can’t talk, read or use tools.

Places and Their Tags

Every place in a mission has one or more tags. Tags are how the world tells you which animals are at home there.

TagWhat it means
DarkUnlit or night-black: alleys, cellars, the woods at midnight.
HighRooftops, walls, trees, beams and ledges.
NarrowVents, pipes, crawlspaces, gaps under doors.
WaterRivers, moats, drains, pools.
OpenLawns, car parks, fields: wide spaces with no cover.
CrowdPeople around, who will notice an animal that doesn’t belong.
LockedDoors, cages, latches and machines.

In animal form, if any of your frame’s Strengths is among the place’s tags, you get +1 die. If any of its Weaknesses is, the roll is at +1 Difficulty. It’s one die and one step at most, however many tags match. If a place has both a Strength and a Weakness of yours, both apply. In human form, tags don’t change your roll.

The Six Frames

Your frame is the kind of animal you become. Your animal is its real size: a moose is as big as a car and a mouse fits in a shoe. Roll a d6 or choose.

d6FrameSneakForceMoveSenseStrengths (+1 die)Weaknesses (+1 Difficulty)
1Big Cats4332Dark, HighWater, Crowd
2Canines3334Open, CrowdHigh
3Birds2144High, OpenNarrow
4Critters4133Narrow, CrowdOpen
5Heavies2433Open, LockedNarrow, Crowd
6Reptiles3333Water, DarkCrowd

Animal-form Wits is always 0. Animal perks work only in animal form.

Big Cats

“You won’t hear me. You won’t see me. Then I’m on the shelf above your head.”

The best sneaks in the game, and good in a fight. Big Cats own the dark and the rooftops, but they hate water and they can’t blend into a crowd: people scream when a jaguar walks into the shop.

Jaguar · Night Rosettes

In Dark places, your Sneak rolls are at −1 Difficulty.

Snow Leopard · Ambush

Your first Strike in each Clash is at −1 Difficulty.

Cheetah · Burst

Once per scene, Push a Move roll without spending Wild.

Canines

“I smelled them before you saw them. They went that way. Come on!”

The best noses in the game, and solid at everything else. Canines run well in the open and pass for somebody’s dog in a crowd, but they’re no climbers.

Coyote · Pack

Once per scene, Help without spending Wild.

Shepherd Dog · Good Dog

In Crowds, your Sneak and Sense rolls are at −1 Difficulty. People see a dog, not you.

Red Fox · Wily

Once per scene, when your roll Fails, it becomes a Partial instead.

Birds

“From up here I can see the whole yard, the guard, the van, and the way out.”

Fast, far-sighted scouts who fly over walls and see everything from above. Birds are no good in a fight and hate tight spaces where they can’t open their wings.

Peregrine Falcon · Keen Eyes

In Open or High places, your Sense rolls are at −1 Difficulty.

Barn Owl · Silent Wings

In Dark places, +1 die on Sneak and Move rolls.

Raven · Clever Beak

Against Locked things you can roll Wits in animal form, with a rating of 2, to work latches, keys and switches. You still can’t talk.

Critters

“Nobody looks down. That’s the whole trick.”

Tiny, quick and everywhere. Critters slip through gaps nothing else fits through and scurry unnoticed under a crowd’s feet. Out in the open, everything wants to eat them, and they can’t fight at all.

House Mouse · Tiny

In Narrow places, your Sneak and Move rolls are at −1 Difficulty.

Brown Rat · Gnaw

Against Locked things, your Force rating is 3.

Grey Squirrel · Leaper

In High places, your Move rolls are at −1 Difficulty.

Heavies

“There was a door. There isn’t now.”

Huge and strong. Heavies break locks by breaking whatever the lock was attached to, and nothing stops them in the open. They don’t fit through anything narrow, and a bison in a crowd is not subtle.

Bison · Shaggy Coat

Once per scene, when you’d take Hurt, take 1 less.

Moose · Antler Sweep

Once per scene, when your Strike against a Beater or Hound Succeeds, it’s out at once.

Hippopotamus · Charge

Once per scene, when a Force roll Succeeds, it counts as a Critical.

Reptiles

“I can wait. I can wait all night.”

Patient all-rounders who are at their best in water and in the dark. People panic when a reptile turns up in a crowd.

Alligator · Lurker

In Water, your Sneak and Force rolls are at −1 Difficulty.

Python · Coil

When your Strike Succeeds, the next roll anyone makes against that threat this Clash is at −1 Difficulty.

Komodo Dragon · Taste the Air

+1 die on Sense rolls, and a Hound’s Tracker doesn’t affect you.

Human Perks

Your human perk is something you were good at before the Wild woke you, and it stays with you in both forms. Every perk works in any form unless it says otherwise. A perk’s extra die counts towards the Cap (Chapter 3). Choose one, or roll two d6: the first die picks the list (1–3 for A, 4–6 for B) and the second picks the row. Two players may have the same human perk.

2nd dieA (first die 1–3)B (first die 4–6)
1Football Player: +1 die on Force rolls.Team Captain: the team starts every mission with 1 Edge.
2Hide-and-Seek Champ: +1 die on Sneak rolls.Animal Whisperer: +1 die on rolls against Hounds, or to get past an obstacle they guard.
3Track Star: +1 die on Move rolls.Swim Team: +1 die on rolls in Water.
4Scout: +1 die on Sense rolls.Gymnast: +1 die on rolls in High places.
5Brainiac (human form): +1 die on Wits rolls.Night Owl: +1 die on rolls in Dark places.
6Gamer: start every mission with 1 extra Wild.Drama Kid: +1 die on rolls in Crowds.

Your Mark

Your Mark is the one thing about you that shows in both shapes: a freckled nose that becomes pale spots on a snout, a white streak of hair that becomes a white patch of fur, a scar through an eyebrow. Friends use it to tell which animal is you. So does the Hunt: when they learn your Mark, you’re Exposed (Chapter 7).

Wild and Hurt

You start every mission with 4 Wild tokens (5 with the Gamer perk) and 0 Hurt, with 3 Hurt boxes on your sheet. Wild is the fuel for everything special you do (Chapter 3). Spend it. Any you don’t spend is lost when the mission ends.

Example: Making Lucía

Lucía’s player rolls a 6 for her frame: Reptiles. Her animal die is a 2, the first animal listed, so she’s an alligator. She puts Sneak 2, Force 1, Move 3, Sense 1, Wits 2 for her human ratings: a fast swimmer and a fast talker. For her perk she rolls 4 and 3: list B, row 3, Swim Team. That gives +1 die on rolls in Water in either form, which suits an alligator very well. Her Mark is the freckles across her nose; as an alligator, they’re a spray of pale spots on her snout. She loves the river path behind the old mill.

Most of the time you just say what your character does, and it happens. You roll only when it’s risky and could go either way: sneaking past a guard, leaping a gap, breaking open a cage. Every roll in the game works the same way.

The Roll

Roll as many d6 as your rating in the approach you’re using, in your current form, plus any bonus dice. Every 5 or 6 is a hit. The Difficulty, usually from 1 to 4, is the number of hits you need.

  • Fail: no hits at all.
  • Partial: at least one hit, but fewer than the Difficulty. You do it, but it costs you something.
  • Success: hits equal to or more than the Difficulty.
  • Critical: a Success with two or more 6s among the dice.

At Difficulty 1, a single hit is a Success, so there’s no Partial. If your rating in an approach is 0, you can’t roll it: an animal can’t roll Wits, for instance. The Storyteller says which approaches work for a problem and the Difficulty of each. Usually there’s more than one way.

Nobody rolls against you. The Storyteller never rolls dice. Guards, Hounds and locks just have a Difficulty, and what they do to you happens when you Fail or get a Partial.

The Cap

Bonus dice come from lots of places: Strengths, perks, friends’ Help and Edges. Some things lower the Difficulty instead. But they don’t pile up forever.

The Cap

From all sources together, one roll gets at most +2 dice and at most −1 Difficulty. Difficulty never goes below 1.

Things that make a roll harder, like a Weakness or a Hound’s Tracker, aren’t limited by the Cap, so a Difficulty can go above 4.

Wild

Wild is the power of your Bond, kept as tokens in front of you. You start each mission with 4. Spend 1 Wild to:

  • Shift into your animal (Chapter 4).
  • Push a roll you just made.
  • Help a friend’s roll.
  • Patch Up 1 Hurt (Chapter 7).

Unspent Wild is lost when the mission ends. Teams that hold their Wild back for later lose far more often than teams that spend it.

Push

Push

After you roll, you may spend 1 Wild to reroll every die that didn’t hit. Keep the new result. You can Push a roll only once. A Push isn’t a bonus die, so the Cap doesn’t limit it.

Help

Help

When a friend at the same obstacle is about to roll, you may spend 1 Wild to give them +1 die. Say how you help. Helping doesn’t use your action, so you can Help and still act yourself. It has to be something your current form can do: in animal form you can’t help with Wits. Help counts towards the Cap (at most +2 dice from everything together), so if the roll already has a bonus die, only one friend’s Help adds anything.

Edges

An Edge is a lucky break the whole team shares. You gain Edges from a Critical when the extra progress isn’t needed (Chapter 5), from a good scouting roll (Chapter 5), and from the Team Captain perk. Spend an Edge for +1 die on anyone’s roll; it counts towards the Cap. The team holds at most 2 Edges at a time; any more are lost. Two Team Captains start the team with 2. Edges you haven’t spent are lost when the mission ends, like Wild.

Order of Things

When a roll happens, the result comes first, then its cost, then everything else. If a Partial both finishes a job and raises the Hunt’s Scent to its Limit, the job is still done before the Hunt comes running (Chapter 5).

The Odds

These are the chances for a single roll before any Push. Pushing a Fail rerolls every die, so it’s a whole second chance.

DiceAt least a PartialSuccess at Difficulty 1at 2at 3Two or more 6s
133%33%———
256%56%11%—3%
370%70%26%4%7%
480%80%41%11%13%
587%87%54%21%20%
691%91%65%32%26%

The lesson: you’ll nearly always get somewhere, but clean Successes against Difficulty 2 or 3 need a good pool, a Strength, a friend’s Help, or a Push.

Example: a Push and a Help

Jonah, as a bison, needs to break the bars of a cage: Force, Difficulty 3. Bison Force is 4. Heavies are strong against Locked things (+1 die), and his Football Player perk adds another (+1 die). Theo offers to Help, but Jonah is already at the Cap of +2 dice, so Theo keeps his Wild. Jonah rolls six dice and gets 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6: two hits, a Partial. He spends 1 Wild to Push and rerolls the four misses: 6, 2, 5, 1. That’s two more hits, four in all, with two 6s. A Critical!

It feels like jumping into cold water and coming up as somebody else, except the somebody else is still you.

When you shift, the Wild wraps around you in a swirl of light and leaves, and a moment later the animal steps out. Nobody sees the in-between, not even you. One second there’s a kid; the next there’s a barn owl blinking on the fence post, wearing that kid’s freckles.

Shifting

  • Shifting into your animal costs 1 Wild and takes your action.
  • Out of Wild? You can still shift into your animal by taking 1 Hurt instead, unless that would put you Down. You pay it as a kid, before you change, so animal perks don’t reduce it.
  • Shifting back to human costs nothing, but it also takes your action.
  • There’s no time limit. Stay an animal all night if you like.

When You Can Shift

Shifting takes your action, so you can shift instead of rolling in a round (Chapter 5). And as you move from one obstacle to the next, everyone may Shift or Patch Up once without it using an action (it still costs the Wild; shifting back counts as a Shift). The gap between scouting and the way in counts as between obstacles. Most shifts happen there, in the gaps between obstacles.

Being Seen

In Sight of the Hunt

Between obstacles you can always find cover, so a shift there is out of sight, unless the mission says you’re being watched. So is a shift you take as your action at an obstacle. A shift during a Clash is always in sight. If the Hunt sees you shift, its Scent rises by 1 (in a Clash, the Clash’s own rise covers it: Chapter 6), and you’re Exposed (Chapter 7).

What Comes With You

  • Your Hurt comes with you. A bruised kid is a bruised fox.
  • Your Wild is yours in either form.
  • Your human perk works in both forms, unless it says human form. You’re still you in there.
  • Your clothes and small personal things (phone, glasses, keys) vanish into the Wild and come back when you do.
  • Anything else you’re holding drops at your feet when you shift. That includes the prize you came to steal.

Being an Animal

In animal form you use your frame’s ratings and your Strengths and Weaknesses (Chapter 2). You’re the real animal at its real size, with its real senses. You also lose some things:

  • You can’t speak, read, or use hands or tools. Your Wits rating is 0, so you can’t roll Wits, or Help a friend’s Wits roll. (The Raven’s Clever Beak lets a Raven roll Wits against Locked things, but even a Raven can’t Help with Wits.)
  • You can carry one small thing in your jaws, beak or claws: a key, a Trophy, a note.
  • You can’t talk to your friends. Bonded don’t share thoughts. Agree on simple signals before a mission: one bark means danger, a tap on the glass means “here”. At the table, of course, the players can talk as much as they like.

Human or Animal?

Shifting is never free, and staying an animal isn’t always best. Before each obstacle, look at what you’ll need:

  • Locked doors and people to talk to are easiest with Wits, and Wits needs human form. (A locked door can also be broken with Force.)
  • Crowds are a Weakness for Big Cats, Heavies and Reptiles. A kid in a crowd is invisible; a jaguar is not.
  • Your Weaknesses can make a human roll the better bet. A cat at the moat might do better swimming as a kid.
  • Everything physical, like sneaking, climbing, fighting and tracking, is usually better as an animal.

A good team spreads out: one or two stay human for the doors and the talking while the others go wild.

Stuck

If you go Down while in animal form (Chapter 7), the Wild holds on to you: you’re Stuck as your animal until the mission ends. You can’t shift back until then. Getting a moose home through town without being seen makes a fine scene for the end of the night.

Example: Choosing Forms

The team reaches the loading bay of the museum: a point obstacle, Dark and Locked, needing 2 progress, with Sneak 3, Force 3 or Wits 2. Maya is already a jaguar: Sneak 4, +1 die for the Dark and +1 for her Hide-and-Seek Champ perk, and Night Rosettes brings the Difficulty down to 2. Six dice against 2 is the team’s best roll, so she slips under the shutter to work it from inside. Priya stays human for the second progress: Wits 3 and her Brainiac perk, four dice against 2. Jonah shifts into his bison on the way, which costs him 1 Wild but no action: Force 4, +1 die for Locked and +1 for his Football Player perk is six dice against 3, ready if the others miss. As a bison he can’t Help Priya’s Wits roll.

Designer’s Note

There’s no countdown on your animal form, and nothing bad happens if you stay too long. The cost of the Wild is paid going in: a token, an action, and everything an animal can’t do. That keeps the choice simple at the table: “Is it worth a Wild to be a bear for this?”

A mission is one night’s work against the Hunt: get in, do the job, get out. The Hunt can smell the Wild. Every slip you make brings them closer, and if they catch your scent before you’re out, the Masters come running.

The Shape of a Mission

  1. The brief. The Storyteller tells you what the Hunt is up to and what you need to do.
  2. Scouting. One of you scouts the place.
  3. The way in. Every mission has two ways in. Scouting decides who picks.
  4. Obstacles. Two to four of them stand between you and the objective.
  5. The objective. Free them, wreck it, or steal it.
  6. The Escape. One or two obstacles on the way out.
  7. The result. Win, Costly Win or Loss.

Players see the mission map and the two ways in. You learn an obstacle’s approaches and Difficulties when you reach it.

Time

  • A round is everyone getting one action: one roll, a shift, a Patch Up, or freeing a friend.
  • A scene is one obstacle, or one Clash. Scouting is a scene too, and when a Clash breaks out at an obstacle, the rest of the obstacle after it is a new scene. “Once per scene” abilities come back at the start of every scene.
  • A mission is the whole night.

Moving from one obstacle to the next is free, and on the way everyone may Shift or Patch Up once without using an action.

Scouting

Scouting

Before going in, one character rolls Sense against the mission’s scouting Difficulty (2 in every mission in this book). Shifting to scout is out of sight, as it is between obstacles; it still costs Wild, but it doesn’t use up the scout’s free Shift before the way in. Friends may Help. Scouting happens outside the place, so it has no tags: Strengths, Weaknesses and place perks don’t count, but a perk for Sense rolls does.

  • Critical: the team picks the way in and gains two Edges.
  • Success: the team picks the way in and gains an Edge.
  • Partial: the team picks the way in, but Scent starts at 1.
  • Fail: the Storyteller picks the way in, and Scent starts at 1.

Obstacles

An obstacle is anything that stands in your way: a guarded gate, a locked door, a dark hall full of Hounds. Each one lists:

  • its tags (Dark, High, Narrow, Water, Open, Crowd, Locked);
  • the approaches that work, with a Difficulty for each;
  • whether it’s a point or a group obstacle, and the progress a point obstacle needs;
  • whether it’s guarded (and by whom) or dangerous.

Point obstacles

One person can deal with it for everyone: a door to unlock, a path to find. Each round, one character rolls (any one of you, and it can be someone different each round) and the others may Help. Progress adds up until the obstacle is cleared, then everyone goes through.

Group obstacles

Everyone has to get past it: a yard to sneak across, a wall to climb. Each round, everyone who isn’t past yet rolls, and each gets past on their own Partial or better. Roll one at a time, in any order; each player decides on a Push before the next one rolls. Those already past can still Help, Patch Up and free a Netted friend. Down and Netted characters can’t roll: when everyone who can act is past, the obstacle is done, and the Down and Netted get up or are freed, or are Taken, as the scene ends (Chapter 7).

Results at an Obstacle

  • Success: 1 progress (or, at a group obstacle, you’re past).
  • Critical: as a Success, plus 1 extra progress. If the extra isn’t needed (always so at a group obstacle), the team gains an Edge instead.
  • Partial: as a Success, but Scent +1.
  • Fail: no progress (you’re not past), and Scent +1. A dangerous obstacle also deals 1 Hurt to whoever Failed.

At a group obstacle, Scent rises once, when the obstacle ends: +1 if anyone got a Partial or a Fail. And from the third round on, if anyone still isn’t past at the end of a round, Scent rises by 1.

In the Escape, Partials cost no Scent. Only Fails count.

Guarded obstacles

Some obstacles have guards: Beaters, Hounds, Trappers or a Huntsman. A Fail at a guarded obstacle starts a Clash with the guards (Chapter 6). You can also choose to start the Clash yourselves, before anyone rolls; then it begins at once. When a Fail starts it at a group obstacle, finish the round’s rolls first, and the obstacle raises Scent for them then (+1 for any Partial or Fail); then the whole team is in the Clash, including anyone already past. The Fail that starts a Clash isn’t a roll against a threat, so it can’t get you Netted. If you beat the guards (or they pull back after round 4), the obstacle is cleared, unless it says progress is still needed. In that case you keep the progress you’ve made and carry on rolling, without the guards.

The team stays together. Everyone takes the same way in and faces the same obstacle at the same time; nobody can run ahead or take the other way.

Scent

The Hunt’s Scent is how close they are to finding you. Track it on the mission tracker, from 0 up to the mission’s Limit. Each mission gives its Limit for 3, 4 and 5 players.

Scent

  • It rises for Partials and Fails at point obstacles, once when a group obstacle ends (and every round it runs from the third on), once at the end of each Clash, for a shift the Hunt can see, for a poor scouting roll, and by 1 at the start of a mission after someone was Exposed. Nothing else raises it.
  • It never goes down. The Limit never changes during a mission.
  • On the Trail: if, when an Escape obstacle begins, Scent is at least half the Limit (round up), that Escape obstacle is at +1 Difficulty for every approach.
  • The Hunt is Up when Scent reaches the Limit. Any Scent past the Limit is lost.

The Hunt Is Up

When Scent reaches the Limit, horns sound across the dark, and the Masters of the Hunt arrive. Nobody fights a Master. You run.

When the Hunt Is Up

  • Finish resolving the roll that did it as if the Hunt weren’t Up yet: if it finished the objective, it’s finished; if it was a Fail at a guarded obstacle, its Clash still starts.
  • From now on, any Fail means you’re Taken, wherever you are. That goes for a Fail in a Clash too, instead of taking Harm. A Fail at a guarded obstacle doesn’t start a Clash any more: you’re just Taken.
  • Anyone still Down or Netted when the scene ends is Taken.
  • If the objective isn’t done, the team chooses: keep going, or Withdraw straight to the Escape (a Loss).
  • If you’re already in the Escape, carry on.

Advice: Press On or Run?

Press on only if you’re already working on the objective. Run the moment a friend is Taken. A Loss can be put right later. A whole team caught at the cage can’t.

The Objective and the Prize

The objective is an obstacle like any other: usually a point obstacle needing 2 or 3 progress, sometimes guarded. When it’s done, the job’s done and you head for the Escape.

Some objectives are a prize to steal, like a Trophy or a ledger. When the objective is done, one character there takes it, with no action, and carries it in hand or in jaws. Handing it to a friend at the same obstacle takes your action, with no roll; between obstacles it’s free. If you shift, it drops at your feet: picking it up takes an action at an obstacle or in a Clash, but between obstacles it’s free. If the carrier is Taken, the prize is lost, and so is the objective. So is a prize nobody is carrying when the last Escape obstacle is behind you.

Withdrawing

The team may Withdraw at any time outside a Clash: give up on the objective and go straight to the Escape. (In a Clash, Slip Away or see it through first.) Withdrawing before the way in just means going home: a Loss, with no Escape to cross. Either way the mission is a Loss, but you live to fight another night.

The Escape

The Escape is one or two group obstacles on the way out. Everyone still free must get past them. Partials cost no Scent here, but Fails do, and if the Hunt is Up, a Fail means you’re Taken. When everyone still free is past the last Escape obstacle, the mission ends.

How It Ends

ResultWhen
WinThe objective is done and nobody is Taken.
Costly WinThe objective is done, but someone (not everyone) is Taken.
LossThe objective isn’t done (you Withdrew, or the prize was lost), or everyone was Taken, even after the objective was done.

When it’s over: unspent Wild and Edges are lost and Hurt clears. In a campaign, the result moves the Hunt track, everyone marks 1 Growth, and Exposed and Taken characters carry over (Chapter 8).

Example: the Hunt Is Up at the Cages

The team is at the cages in Pemberton’s Pets: Wits 2 or Force 3, 3 progress. The Limit for four players is 6, and Scent is already 5. They have 2 progress. Priya rolls Wits and gets a Partial: 1 progress, the cages spring open, and Scent +1 reaches the Limit. The result comes first, so the cages are open before the Hunt is Up. Horns sound outside. The objective is done, so there’s no choice to make: run! In the Escape, every Fail now means Taken, so the team spends every Wild token it has left on Help and Pushes.

Sometimes sneaking fails, and sometimes a wall of grey Hounds just won’t let you by. A Clash is a fight: quick, loud, and over in a few rounds. Clashes are noisy, so the Hunt always hears them.

Threats

Everyone you fight is a threat with three numbers:

  • Difficulty: the hits you need to land a blow on it, slip it, or distract it.
  • Toughness: how much harm it takes before it’s out (knocked down, chased off or tied up).
  • Harm: how much Hurt it deals to you.

Some threats also have a special rule. All of them are in Chapter 10. Threats never roll; they hurt you when you slip up.

A Round of a Clash

Each round, everyone in the Clash takes one action, in any order the players like:

Clash Actions

  • Strike (Force) a threat. Success: 1 harm. Critical: 2 harm. When a threat has taken harm equal to its Toughness, it’s out.
  • Distract (Sneak or Move) a threat. A Success puts the next Strike against it this round at −1 Difficulty.
  • Slip Away (Move or Sneak) from a threat. A Success takes you out of the Clash. At a group obstacle you’re past it; at a point obstacle you wait, out of harm’s way, until the Clash ends.
  • Shift, Patch Up, or free a Netted friend (no roll).

A Critical on Distract or Slip Away works like a Success; Edges come only from obstacles.

Against a threat, a Partial does the job, but the threat’s Harm hits you. A Fail just hits you.

At the end of each round, each threat that nobody rolled against deals its Harm to one character in the Clash, chosen by the Storyteller.

You can Help a friend’s roll in a Clash just as anywhere else: 1 Wild for +1 die, without using your action. Edges work too.

That last rule matters. Leave a Hound alone and it bites someone. Every threat needs somebody rolling against it, even if that’s just a Critter Distracting it so the bison can Strike.

How a Clash Ends

The End of a Clash

A Clash ends when every threat is out; at the end of round 4, when any threats still standing pull back to wait for the Masters; or when nobody who can act is left in it (everyone has slipped away or is Down, Netted or Taken), and then the guards are still there.

When a Clash ends, Scent rises once: +1, or +2 if it reached round 4, someone went Down, or someone shifted during it. Anyone who shifted during it is Exposed.

The Clash’s Scent rises first; then the scene ends. Down and Netted friends get back up if anyone is still standing (slipping away counts) and the Hunt isn’t Up (Chapter 7); so if that rise brings the Hunt Up, they’re Taken. If the Clash started at a guarded obstacle, beating the guards (or seeing them pull back) clears it, unless the obstacle still needs progress. If it ended because nobody was left, the guards are still on guard: at a group obstacle, those who slipped away are past; at a point obstacle, the next Fail there starts a new Clash with them.

Fighting Smart

  • Shift before the fight, not during it. If an obstacle is guarded, decide on the way there who’s going to be the bison. Shifting mid-Clash costs your action, raises the Clash’s Scent to +2, and Exposes you.
  • Pick on one threat at a time. A Hound with 1 Toughness left is still biting.
  • Small animals Distract. A mouse can’t Strike for much, but a Distract on a Hound’s nose makes the big friend’s Strike much easier.
  • Get it done in three rounds. Round 4 costs an extra Scent.
  • Sometimes don’t fight at all. Slip Away is a fine choice when the objective is somewhere else.

Example: Two Hounds on the Lawn

The Hound patrol crosses a dark, open lawn (Open, Dark). Lucía is the last to roll that round and Fails to sneak past, and two Hounds turn: Difficulty 2, Toughness 3, Harm 1. The team was ready: Jonah and Theo shifted on the way in.

Round 1. Priya the barn owl Distracts the first Hound by swooping at its face. She rolls Move: Bird Move 4, +1 die for the Open lawn (a Bird Strength) and +1 die for Silent Wings in the Dark, six dice against Difficulty 2. A Success. Jonah the bison Strikes that Hound: Force 4, +1 die for the Open lawn and +1 for his Football Player perk, against Difficulty 1 thanks to the Distract. A Success: 1 harm. Theo the coyote Strikes the second Hound with four dice (Force 3, +1 for the Open lawn) against Difficulty 2 and gets one hit, a Partial: 1 harm, and the Hound bites back for 1 Hurt. Lucía the alligator Strikes the first Hound with four dice (Force 3, +1 for the Dark, a Reptile Strength): a Success. Both Hounds were rolled against, so neither attacks at the end of the round.

Round 2. The first Hound has 1 Toughness left, the second 2. Jonah Strikes the second and rolls a Critical: 2 harm, and it’s out. Lucía Strikes the first and Succeeds: it’s out too.

Before the Clash began, Lucía’s Fail raised Scent by 1 for the lawn. The Clash ends in round 2. Nobody went Down and nobody shifted during it, so it raises Scent by 1 more, and beating the guards clears the lawn.

Things go wrong. Hounds bite, nets fly, and sometimes a friend doesn’t make it out. Nobody in Second Nature dies. The worst that happens is being Taken, and a Taken friend can always be rescued. Here is everything that can go wrong, from a scraped knee to a cage.

Hurt

Hurt

Everyone has 3 Hurt boxes, the same in every form. Mark one for each point of Hurt you take. Hurt never lowers your dice: a bruised kid rolls as well as a fresh one. All Hurt clears between missions.

You take Hurt from a threat’s Harm (Chapter 6), from Failing at a dangerous obstacle (Chapter 5), and from shifting with no Wild left (Chapter 4).

Patch Up

Spend 1 Wild and your action to heal 1 Hurt, yours or a friend’s. You can also Patch Up once on the way between obstacles without using an action (instead of shifting). Patching Up a Down friend lowers their Hurt, but they stay Down until the scene ends.

Down

Down

When your third Hurt box is marked, you’re Down. You can’t act until the scene ends.

When the scene ends, if a friend is still standing and the Hunt isn’t Up, you get back up with 2 Hurt and you’re past the obstacle: your friends carried you. Otherwise you’re Taken.

If you go Down in animal form, you’re Stuck: you can’t shift back until the mission ends.

Netted

Netted

When you Fail against a Trapper, you’re Netted instead of Hurt. You can’t act until a friend spends their action to free you (no roll). When the scene ends, you’re freed if a friend is still standing and the Hunt isn’t Up; otherwise you’re Taken.

Taken

Taken

You’re Taken:

  • when you Fail while the Hunt is Up;
  • when you’re Down or Netted at the end of a scene and nobody is standing to help, or the Hunt is Up.

The Hunt cages you, and you’re out for the rest of the mission. If you were carrying the prize, it’s lost. You’re also Exposed.

A Taken player isn’t out of the game. In a one-shot, they can describe what they see from the cage, and it’s worth remembering for later. In a campaign, the next mission can be the rescue (Chapter 8).

Exposed

You’re Exposed when the Hunt sees you shift, or Takes you. They know your face and your Mark now. In a campaign, an Exposed character’s next mission starts at Scent 1, because the Hunt is watching your house. That’s only ever 1: it doesn’t add to a poor scouting roll’s Scent 1.

Everyone at Once

If every character is Down, Netted or Taken at the same moment, nobody is left to help: everyone is Taken, and the mission is a Loss.

Giving Up

You can always Withdraw: abandon the objective and head straight for the Escape (Chapter 5). It’s a Loss, but on the way out the only way to be Taken is the usual one: a Fail once the Hunt is Up, or being left Down or Netted. Withdrawing is never better than winning, but it beats being caught.

Telling It Kindly

Describe being Taken the way a good adventure film would: a net drops, a gilded cage clicks shut, and a voice in the dark says, “Well, well. Another one.” Keep it tense, never cruel. Being Taken is a cliffhanger, and the rescue is the next chapter.

One mission makes a great evening. A campaign tells the whole story: six missions against the Gilded Hunt, each one bringing you closer to the seventh, the night of the Last Hunt, when the Masters will try to chain the Old Wild for good.

The Hunt Track

The Hunt Track

The campaign has one Hunt track, from 0 to 6, on the mission tracker. It starts at 0.

  • After a Win, it doesn’t move.
  • After a Costly Win, it rises by 1.
  • After a Loss, it rises by 2.

When it reaches 6, the Last Hunt comes early: the next mission is the Last Hunt. Otherwise the Last Hunt is the seventh mission. The track never goes down.

Growth

Growth

After every mission, whatever the result, every character marks 1 Growth. When you reach 2, 4 and 6 Growth, choose one:

  • +1 Wild: start every mission with 1 more Wild, to a maximum of 6, counting the Gamer perk.
  • A second human perk (a different one).
  • +1 to a human rating, to a maximum of 3.
  • Wild Sense: choose one of your frame’s Strengths. It now works in human form too.

You can’t choose the same thing twice, except +1 to a human rating (for a different rating each time).

Your Bond grows; your animal doesn’t change. You keep one animal for life.

Exposed

If anyone ended a mission Exposed, the Hunt is watching the team. The next mission starts at Scent 1 (only 1, however many of you were Exposed). After that mission, Exposed clears.

Taken Friends

A Taken character is held by the Hunt. The Hunt means to bind their Bond into a new Trophy on the next full moon: in a campaign, the rescue can come on either of the next two missions, and after that it’s too late. Rescuing them can be the team’s next mission (The Lodge on the Hill, Chapter 17, is written as a rescue), or a Storyteller can add the rescue to another mission as one more point obstacle before the Escape: a locked cage, Force 3 or Wits 2, 3 progress, guarded or not. A Taken character marks Growth after the mission like everyone else.

While a character is Taken, their player makes a new Bonded (or takes a ready-made one) who joins at the start of the next mission, never during one. A new character starts with Growth equal to the lowest in the group. When a Taken friend is rescued, their player chooses which of their two characters to play from then on; the other becomes a friend of the team.

If a Taken friend isn’t rescued before the full moon, the Hunt makes their Trophy. They lose their Bond and become a normal kid again, but they remember everything. Freeing that Trophy from the Hunt gives them their Bond back; the Storyteller can make that a mission of its own.

Everyone Taken

If the whole team is Taken, play a Breakout next: every player makes a new Bonded (or takes a ready-made one), and the new team runs The Lodge on the Hill to free the old one. The new characters start with the old team’s lowest Growth. The Breakout comes first even if the Hunt track has just reached 6: the Last Hunt follows it.

The Last Hunt

The Last Hunt is the campaign’s final mission, on the night the Masters gather to chain the Old Wild. Build it as a Hard mission (Chapter 12) at the place the campaign has been leading to. The higher the Hunt track, the harder it gets: if the Hunt track is 4 or more, lower the mission’s Limit by 1. Win it, or win it at a cost, and the Old Wild stays free, the Trophies break, and every Bonded animal the Hunt ever took runs home (a friend Taken that night is freed with them). Lose it, and the story isn’t over, but the world has become a much tamer place.

Designer’s Note

The campaign rules in this chapter haven’t been simulated yet; the five missions in Part Three have. Expect Growth, the Hunt track and the Last Hunt to change after playtesting. If something feels off at your table, tell us.

Between Missions

Between missions, you’re kids again: school, homework, families who wonder why you’re so tired. You don’t need rules for this. A few minutes of play between missions, such as spotting a Huntsman at the school gate or hearing a rumour at the shops, is a good way to lead into the next brief.

As the Storyteller, you are the town, the Hunt, the night, and every voice that isn’t a player’s. You describe what the Bonded see, smell and hear; you say when a roll is needed and how hard it is; and you play the Hunt fairly but without mercy. You never roll dice. Your job is to set problems; the players’ job is to solve them.

The First Night

Before Everyone Arrives (about 15 minutes)

  • Print the six ready-made Bonded (Chapter 18) or one blank character sheet per player, one mission tracker, the Storyteller’s round card, and the At the Table page (Part Four).
  • Gather six d6 per player and about six Wild tokens each, plus a marker for the Scent track.
  • Read Pemberton’s Pets (Chapter 13), the Easy mission. Note its Limit for your number of players.

At the Table (about 15 minutes)

  1. Talk about the feel (two minutes): see “Keeping It Fun” below.
  2. Hand out characters. Each player takes a ready-made Bonded. If two players want the same one, they roll a die: the higher roll chooses first (roll again on a tie). A player who’d rather make their own does it now, with Chapter 2’s steps; allow ten minutes.
  3. Explain the roll with one practice roll each: three dice against Difficulty 2. Count the 5s and 6s, and compare them to the Difficulty.
  4. Give everyone 4 Wild (5 for a Gamer) and explain the four ways to spend it.
  5. Read the brief and start.

Players don’t read the mission pages. Show them the map and the two ways in; tell them an obstacle’s approaches and Difficulties when they reach it.

Running an Obstacle

  1. Describe it, with its tags: “The shop floor is pitch dark. The watchman is asleep by the counter.”
  2. Say what works: “Sneak or Move, Difficulty 2. It’s a group obstacle: everyone has to get past.”
  3. Ask who does what. Let the players decide forms, who rolls and who Helps.
  4. Resolve the rolls: result first, then its cost.
  5. Mark Scent as the rules say, and describe the change: a dog barks two streets away; a light comes on upstairs.

If a player wants to try something that isn’t on the obstacle’s list, pick the nearest approach and Difficulty from the list. Don’t make up a new approach that skips the obstacle: every way through is a roll.

Running a Clash

Use the round card in Part Four. It has four steps:

A Clash Round

  1. Everyone in the Clash takes one action, in any order the players like. Help can come at any time.
  2. Resolve each roll as it’s made: result, then Harm.
  3. Each threat nobody rolled against this round hurts one character of your choice.
  4. Check the end: every threat out, nobody left, or the end of round 4. Then raise Scent once: +1, or +2 if it reached round 4, someone went Down, or someone shifted during it.

When a threat attacks someone, choose fairly. Pick whoever the threat would really go for, such as the one who just hit it or the one closest to it, rather than always the weakest.

The Scent Track

Keep the Scent track where everyone can see it. The Hunt closing in should be a shared, growing dread, not a secret. When Scent reaches half the Limit, tell the players: “They’re On the Trail. The way out will be harder.” When it reaches the Limit, make it big: horns, lights, the baying of Hounds. The Hunt is Up.

Making Rulings

The rules don’t cover everything. When something comes up:

  • Choose the reading nearest to what the rules already say, and say it out loud so everyone knows.
  • Never make a roll free. No plan, perk or trick lets anyone skip an obstacle without a roll.
  • Write it down and keep that ruling for the rest of the campaign. We’d love to hear about it too.

Keeping It Fun

This game is for ages 10 and up. Some players will want the Hunt to be properly scary; others won’t. Before the first mission, ask:

  • Is there anything nobody wants in the game? Snakes, spiders, cages, the dark. Take it out or keep it off-screen.
  • How scary should the Hunt be? Creepy-and-cold, or bluster-and-moustache?

During play, anyone can say “pause” at any time, for any reason, and the game stops while you talk. Then carry on, change direction, or skip ahead. Nobody has to explain why.

Keep the violence light. Hits are scrapes and bruises; a threat that’s “out” is knocked over, chased off or tangled in its own net. Nobody bleeds and nobody dies.

Giving Every Animal Its Moment

Look at the team’s frames before a mission, and notice the tags. A mission with no Water gives an alligator little to do; one with no Narrow gaps leaves a mouse on the bench. The missions in this book spread their tags so that every frame has a place to shine. When you build your own (Chapter 12), do the same.

Pacing

  • One roll at a time at a point obstacle. If someone fancies a turn, let them have the next round.
  • Move quickly between obstacles. A sentence of description, then the next problem.
  • Remind players to spend Wild. Every token left at the end is wasted.
  • A mission takes two to three hours. If you’re running long, it’s fine to describe the last stretch of the Escape after its final roll.

“Every wild thing has a price. Most of them simply haven’t been asked yet.” — overheard at the Lodge on Thornhill

The Gilded Hunt is older than the town, older than the roads, older than anyone’s great-grandmother’s stories. It began as a club of rich hunters who found out, long ago, that a Bonded animal caught alive and bound in gold gives up its gift to whoever wears the gold. They have been collecting ever since.

What the Hunt Wants

The Hunt wants the Wild itself. Every Trophy they make is a little piece of it, chained. For three hundred years they have been preparing for the Last Hunt: one night, under the right moon, when the Masters gather and bind the Old Wild for good. After that, every animal on Earth would obey whoever holds the leash, and the Hunt means to hold it. The people would follow soon after.

The Old Wild knows. That’s why it woke the Bonded.

Who They Are

Members of the Hunt are respectable. They sit on the museum board, own the mill, sponsor the zoo, give prizes at the school sports day. They are polite, generous and charming, and they never, ever talk about the Hunt in daylight. Nobody joins by accident. You’re invited, you’re tested, and you swear.

  • Masters lead the Hunt. Each wears several Trophies. They rarely leave the Lodge, and when they do, it’s because the Hunt is Up.
  • Huntsmen are full members. Each has earned one Trophy.
  • Beaters are hired hands: watchmen, drivers, “estate staff”. Most of them don’t know what the Hunt really is, and don’t want to.
  • Trappers are the Hunt’s specialists in catching things alive, with nets and cages.
  • Hounds are the Hunt’s own breed: tall, grey and silent, with gilt collars and noses that can smell the Wild.

Trophies

A Trophy is a Bonded animal’s gift, bound into a piece of gold: a ring, a brooch, a cane-head, a locket. Whoever wears it borrows that animal’s best sense or strength. Every Trophy was once somebody’s Bond. Break one, and the Bond goes free.

TrophyWhat it lends
Hawkseye RingEyes that see a mouse move at the far end of a field.
Wolfnose BroochA nose that can follow yesterday’s footsteps.
Owl’s-Ear EarringsHearing that catches a whisper through a wall.
Bearpaw CaneStrength to lift a car door off its hinges.
Stag-Heart LocketLegs that never tire.
Snakeskin GlovesHands that sense warmth in the dark.

In play, a Huntsman’s Trophy makes them hard to sneak past (below). What it looks like and what it lends is up to you.

How the Hunt Finds You

The Hunt can smell the Wild. When the Bonded slip up, make noise, fight or shift in sight, the Hunt’s Scent grows (Chapter 5). The Hounds track it; the Trophies sharpen it; and when it’s strong enough, the Masters come. Between missions the Hunt is patient: it watches Exposed children, asks friendly questions at the school gate, and waits.

What the Hunt Does With the Taken

The Taken are caged, gently and coldly, like prize animals. The Hunt doesn’t hurt them; it needs them whole. At the next full moon, a Master binds the Taken child’s Bond into new gold. Until then, they can be rescued.

Wrenfield is a small river town with one high street, one cinema, two schools and a hill nobody climbs. You can play in your own town instead (it’s more fun when you know the streets), but Wrenfield is where the missions in this book take place, and it’s ready to use.

Wrenfield. The five missions in Part Three take place at the numbered places.

The Night of the Waking

Last October a storm knocked out every light in Wrenfield for one hour. In that hour the zoo’s fences failed, animals got loose all over town, and six children each found themselves face to face with one of them. By morning the animals were back in their pens or gone into the woods, and the children were Bonded. Most people remember it as “the night the zoo got out”. The Hunt remembers it very differently.

Places

1. Pemberton’s Pets

A cramped old pet shop at the end of the High Street. Old Mrs Pemberton ran it for forty years and sold it last spring to a polite company nobody had heard of. The new manager, Mr Rook, keeps odd hours, and the strays of Wrenfield have started to disappear. Mission: Chapter 13.

2. Wrenfield Zoo

A small, much-loved zoo by the river, with a moat, an aviary and a famous pair of snow leopards. Since the night of the Waking, its director, Dr Imogen Hale, has hired new “transport staff” who work only at night. Mission: Chapter 14.

3. The Old Mill

A tall brick mill on the River Wren, with a working waterwheel the town keeps for show. Its owner, Mr Corwin Thatch, has been building something in the tower. The Hounds have been restless ever since. Mission: Chapter 15.

4. The Ashcombe Museum

Wrenfield’s natural history museum: dark halls of stuffed animals, a dinosaur skeleton, and a glass case of “historic hunting jewellery” that is never quite the same twice. Once a year it hosts a grand gala for its patrons. Mission: Chapter 16.

5. The Lodge on Thornhill

A great stone house on the wooded hill above the town, behind a deer park and a high wall. It belongs to Lady Cordelia Vane, Master of the Hunt in Wrenfield, though in town she’s known only as a generous patron of the museum and the zoo. Mission: Chapter 17.

Elsewhere in Town

  • The High Street: the chip shop, the bakery, the cinema, and the bus stop where everyone meets.
  • Wrenfield Library: warm, quiet, and full of old maps. The librarian, Ms Dara Quill, has been reading about the Hunt for years and is the closest thing the Bonded have to an adult ally.
  • Wrenwood: the woods between the town and Thornhill, full of badgers, owls and old paths. A good place to shift unseen.
  • The River Wren: slow and brown, with a towpath, a weir by the mill, and drains that run under half the town.
  • Wrenfield Middle School: where most of the Bonded spend their days, trying to stay awake.

Once you’ve played the missions in Part Three, you’ll want your own: the Hunt at the swimming baths, the Hunt at the school fair, the Hunt in your actual town. This chapter shows how to build one that plays well. The shape is always the same: two ways in, a few obstacles, an objective, and a way out.

The Checklist

Every Mission Has

  • A brief: what the Hunt is doing and what the team must do: free, wreck or steal.
  • A map that matches the obstacles, place by place.
  • Two ways in with different tags and approaches, so they suit different forms and scouting matters.
  • Two to four obstacles inside, then the objective.
  • One or two Escape obstacles, each with at least two approaches, so no team is stuck without a way out.
  • For every obstacle: its tags, every approach that works and its Difficulty, point or group, the progress needed, and any guards or danger.
  • Stats for every threat (use Chapter 10).
  • A Limit for 3, 4 and 5 players, and a label (Easy, Standard or Hard).
  • A scouting Difficulty (2 unless the place is unusually hard to watch).
  • Who arrives if the Hunt is Up (a Master, and who brings them).
  • After the Mission: what a Win, a Costly Win and a Loss each change in town.
  • At least one moment for human form: someone to talk past, a lock to work, a crowd to blend into.

Choosing Obstacles

Give most obstacles two or three approaches, so different animals can solve them in different ways. A wall might be Move 2 (climb or fly it), Sneak 3 (find the gap) or Force 3 (break through). Then give it tags, and think about who they favour:

TagStrong hereWeak here
DarkBig Cats, Reptiles—
HighBig Cats, BirdsCanines
NarrowCrittersBirds, Heavies
WaterReptilesBig Cats
OpenCanines, Birds, HeaviesCritters
CrowdCanines, CrittersBig Cats, Heavies, Reptiles
LockedHeavies—

Across a mission, try to use every tag at least once, and don’t let one tag take over. A mission that is all rooftops is a mission for birds.

Difficulty

  • 1: routine, for a quick roll that rarely goes wrong.
  • 2: the normal Difficulty for anything worth rolling.
  • 3: hard, the approach that works but isn’t the obvious one.
  • 4: almost never on its own; Weaknesses and Trackers will push some rolls there anyway.

Point or group?

If one person could deal with it for everyone (open a door, find the path), make it a point obstacle needing 1 to 3 progress. If everyone has to get past it themselves (cross a yard, climb a wall), make it a group obstacle. Group obstacles are harder with more players, point obstacles easier; that’s what the per-size Limit is for.

Guards and danger

Guard one or two obstacles per mission: a Beater at the door, two Hounds on the lawn, a Huntsman at the objective. A dangerous obstacle (a fast river, a high beam) deals 1 Hurt on a Fail. Use it where a fall or a current makes sense.

Setting the Limit

The Limit and the obstacles together make a mission Easy, Standard or Hard. The five missions in Part Three were tested thousands of times, with groups of 3, 4 and 5, so their Limits hit their labels. For a new mission:

  1. Count the obstacles the team will face: one way in, every obstacle inside, the objective, and each Escape obstacle. (Pemberton’s Pets has 5; the Lodge on the Hill has 7.)
  2. Choose the label from the obstacles. Easy: Difficulty 2 nearly everywhere, at most one guarded obstacle, no Huntsman. Standard: a Difficulty 3 or two, two guarded obstacles, one Escape obstacle. Hard: two Escape obstacles, and guards that bite: a Huntsman, three Hounds together, or three guarded obstacles.
  3. The Limit for 3 players is the number of obstacles plus 2 for an Easy or Standard mission, or the number of obstacles for a Hard one. Use the same Limit for 4 and 5 players.
  4. Play it, and adjust. If the Hunt is Up in nearly every game, add 1; if it’s never close, take 1 away. If bigger groups find it easy, take 1 off their Limit only.

Step 3 gives every mission in Part Three its Limit for 3 players. Their Limits for 4 and 5 players came from testing.

Designer’s Note

Steps 2 to 4 are a rule of thumb, not something we’ve tested beyond the five missions in this book. A mission’s label should come from how it actually plays, not from what you meant it to be. If your Easy mission keeps going wrong, it’s a Standard mission, and that’s fine.
